newsitem.title: USA: Army sex case lawyer threatens top brass.
newsitem.headline: Army sex case lawyer threatens top brass.

text.p: A lawyer for the Army's senior enlisted man threatened Wednesday to disclose sexual misconduct by top brass if the Army court-martials his client on similar charges.
"We will open up all of the Army's dirty laundry if this case goes to trial. And that's a promise," Charles Gittins said on behalf of Gene McKinney, whose rank is Sergeant Major of the Army.

McKinney, the Army's highest-ranking non-commissioned officer, is facing 22 preliminary charges, including adultery, assault, maltreatment of subordinates, communication of threats and obstruction of justice.

McKinney has denied all charges and said the investigation now under way was racially motivated. All six of his accusers are white women; he is black. If convicted, he faces a maximum possible prison sentence of 57-1/2 years.
Gittins told reporters outside a hearing room at Ft. McNair that the army was operating on a double standard that had let higher-ups muster out quietly to dodge prosecution on sex-related charges.

McKinney, a 29-year Army veteran, serves as chief advocate for the Army's 410,000 enlisted troops. He has applied for retirement with full benefits. Hearings have been under way in his case for seven weeks to determine whether the Army has enough evidence to go ahead with a court-martial.
Gittins, in a telephone interview with Reuters, accused the Army of mounting a "selective, vindictive, discriminatory" investigation of McKinney, marked by racism.

"We are aware of a number of senior officers -- colonels and above, who also happen to be white -- who have engaged in misconduct of the type that is charged on the charge sheet against Sergeant Major McKinney," he said.
He said he had information implicating up to a dozen officers on charges including adultery, harassment, and making unwanted sexual advances.

"And in point of fact they have not been prosecuted. They in fact haven't really been seriously investigated," Gittins maintained. He said the alleged offenders had been allowed to retire quietly "rather than to put the Army through the embarrassment of those kind of situations."
Gittins said that if the case went to trial, McKinney, who in the past had credited the Army with racial fairness, would be at war with the Army.
"And he's not going to be constrained by caring about the institution of the Army. At that point, the Army is just something that's trying to hurt him."
"We will do whatever we have to do to get Gene McKinney acquitted within the bounds of the law," he added.
An Army spokeswoman, Martha Rudd, declined comment on the threat to expose the Army's supposed dirty laundry, saying the service would not comment on judicial proceedings.
William Perry, who retired as Defense secretary at the start of President Clinton's second administration in January, testified as a character witness on behalf of McKinney Wednesday.
Testifying by telephone, the former Pentagon chief said he had been surprised to learn of the allegations against McKinney, the first black to achieve that rank.
